product.title: Brazilian Portuguese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 in Brazilian Portuguese: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Portuguese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. This is the Portuguese actually spoken in Brazil — você, the -ndo form, and the way real Brazilians talk, not the textbook forms that only live in grammar books. Questions keep normal word order (no do/does), adjectives you'll recognize from Spanish or English, and each unit tackles one real hurdle: noun gender, ser vs estar, and verbs that change with every person and tense.

blocks.text: Portuguese has more than two hundred and sixty million speakers, and over three quarters of them live in **one country**: Brazil. This course teaches the Portuguese spoken there — not the Portuguese of Lisbon, and not the formal standard that only lives inside grammar books.

That choice shows up on almost every page. You won't learn *tu falas*, because Brazilians say **você fala**. You won't learn *estou a comer*, because in Brazil it's **estou comendo**. And you'll be taught to say *eu vi ele* — a form a teacher in Portugal would circle in red, but one that a hundred million Brazilians say every day.

Here's some good news beginners rarely hear. Portuguese has one big gift for English speakers: **questions don't change their word order**. *Você é americano?* has exactly the same word order as *Você é americano.* — only your voice rises at the end. There's no *do you*, no flipping the verb in front of the subject. You can ask a question the way you'd ask "You're American?" in casual English, and it's perfectly correct.

A second gift, if you know any Spanish, French or Italian: **adjectives usually come after the noun**. *Um carro vermelho* = "a car red". English speakers keep wanting to write *um vermelho carro*; a little attention in the first week fixes that habit for good.

So the difficulties lie elsewhere, and this course doesn't hide them. There are three: **noun gender** — every noun is masculine or feminine, tables and doors included; **verbs that change form** depending on who does the action and when, far more than English *speak/speaks/spoke*; and **two verbs for "to be"**, *ser* and *estar*, where picking the wrong one changes the meaning.
None of the three is put off. Gender comes in unit 2, *ser* versus *estar* gets a whole unit to itself in unit 3, and verb endings start in unit 6 and are built up bit by bit until the last unit.
The explanations are deliberately short. What's long isn't the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.

Read out loud from the very first unit. Brazilian Portuguese has sounds English spelling won't prepare you for — an **r** at the start of a word sounds like an **h**, and an **l** at the end of a syllable turns into a **w**. Neither will ever reach your ears if you only read silently.

Every time you note down a new noun, **write it with its article**: not *mesa*, but *a mesa*; not *livro*, but *o livro*. Ten seconds per word, and the whole gender question sorts itself out behind the scenes.

Don't wait until your accent is perfect before you dare to speak. Brazilians are among the most generous people in the world toward foreigners who try their language — your mistakes will be met with a smile, not a correction.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Boa sorte, e vamos lá!*
This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — read the Portuguese out loud first, without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the translation. It's the part people skip most, yet it's where you see how Portuguese *thinks*. Example: *Quantos anos você tem?* literally means "how-many years you have?", not "how old are you".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange a moment ago.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, with their pronunciation.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: Spaced review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier one — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Portuguese, look at the English, and rebuild the Portuguese sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Nouns are always written with their article — *o livro*, *a mesa* — and you're asked to memorize them that way. Gender can't be guessed from meaning; it has to stick to the word from the first time you meet it.

If you've already learned a word without its article, don't guess from its meaning. Use the rough rules: ending in **-o** is usually *o*, ending in **-a** is usually *a*, ending in **-ção** is always *a*. The rest are learned one by one — and there are fewer of them than you fear.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Brazilian Portuguese is a language where sound matters far more than spelling — *de* is said "jee", *noite* is said "NOY-chee", *Brasil* is said "brah-ZEEW". If you only read with your eyes, you'll memorize a language nobody in Brazil will recognize.

This is the most important section of the whole course, and it's worth reading carefully once before unit 1. The **Say it** column in every table uses English-style spelling: *ah* as in *father*, *eh* as in *bed*, *ay* as in *say*, *ee* as in *see*, *oh* as in *go*, *aw* as in *law*, *oo* as in *food*, *ow* as in *now*, *oy* as in *boy*, *y* as in *my* (on its own: *eye*). **Capital letters** mark the stressed syllable.
The good news: once you know the list below, Portuguese spelling becomes **very predictable**. Unlike English, a letter is almost always read the same way in the same position.
Eight sounds that change everything
If you only have time to learn one table in this whole course, learn this one. These eight rows are the biggest difference between "understood" and "not understood" in Brazil.

blocks.title: Three words that prove it
items: *Rio de Janeiro* is said **HEE-oo jee zhah-NEY-roo** — not "ree-oh day ja-nay-ro". The R at the front becomes H, *de* becomes *jee*, *J* becomes *zh*, and the final *-o* becomes *oo*.
*Brasil* is said **brah-ZEEW** — the S between vowels becomes Z, the final L becomes a W glide. There's no "l" sound at the end of that word at all.
*obrigado* is said **oh-bree-GAH-doo**. If you say "oh-bree-GAH-doh", you'll still be understood — but you'll sound like you're reading, not talking.

blocks.text: Vowels: open and closed

The letters **e** and **o** each have two sounds, and Portuguese marks them with different accents. The acute accent (**é, ó**) means an open mouth; the circumflex (**ê, ô**) means a more closed mouth. The **Say it** column keeps them apart: é = **eh**, ê = **ay**, ó = **aw**, ô = **oh**.

head: Letter

rows: closed **ay** — as in *say*, but without the glide

blocks.text: Look at the last pair in that table: *avó* (grandmother) and *avô* (grandfather) differ **only** in the shape of the accent. One little hat, one little slash — and the person changes sex. This isn't a rare case; they're among the most common words in any family conversation.
Nasal vowels: the tilde and m/n

This is the most typical sound of Portuguese, the one that keeps it from sounding like Spanish. The vowel is nasalized — the air comes out through your nose — and that happens in two cases: when there's a tilde (**ã, õ**), or when the vowel is followed by **m** or **n** at the end of a syllable.

blocks.text: The **n** in the Say it column **is not pronounced as a full n** — your tongue doesn't touch the roof of your mouth. It's only a sign that the vowel before it comes out through your nose. The easiest way to practice: say the English word "song" and stop just before the back of your tongue closes. The humming vowel left over is a nasal vowel.

blocks.title: One word that always surprises
items: *muito* (very, a lot) is written without any nasal mark, yet it's said **MOOYN-too** — with a nasal vowel in the middle. It's the only common word that behaves this way, and it happens to be one of the words you'll use most.
*bem* and *bom* differ in meaning and in sound: *bem* (BAYN) means "well" for states (*tudo bem*), *bom* (BOHN) means "good" as a masculine adjective (*bom dia*).

blocks.text: Stress rules: just three lines

Stress in Portuguese doesn't always fall in the same place, but the rules are short and almost exception-free. One more thing to know first: an **r** at the end of a syllable is a light, breathy **h** in Rio and São Paulo, written **hh** after a vowel in the Say it column (*falar* fah-LAHH, *tarde* TAHH-jee). Don't roll it, and don't say an American r.

items: **Is there an accent mark?** That's where the stress is. Done. *café* → kah-FEH, *português* → pohh-too-GAYS, *fácil* → FAH-seew.
**Ending in a, e, o, m, s** (no accent) → stress on the **next-to-last** syllable: *casa* → KAH-zah, *falam* → FAH-lown, *livros* → LEE-vroos.
**Ending in any other letter** (i, u, l, r, z, ã, ão) → stress on the **last** syllable: *falar* → fah-LAHH, *Brasil* → brah-ZEEW, *irmã* → eeh-MAHN.

blocks.text: Because of the second rule, almost every Portuguese word is stressed on the next-to-last syllable, since almost every word ends in *a*, *e* or *o*. If you're unsure and there's no accent, guess there — you'll be right far more often than wrong.
These pages aren't study material — they're a place for a quick look when you forget a form in the middle of an exercise. Everything here was explained slowly in its own unit.

Also: *em + um* = **num**, *em + uma* = **numa**, *de + ele* = **dele**, *de + ela* = **dela**, *em + esse* = **nesse**, *de + aquele* = **daquele**.
3. Possessives (unit 5)
4. Ser vs estar (units 1, 3)
**ser** for identity, origin, profession, characteristics, time, possession. **estar** for location, feelings, physical states, today's weather, and things in progress.
5. Regular verbs, present tense (units 6, 7)
6. Past tense (unit 15)
7. Imperfeito — the describing past (unit 17)
Only four are irregular: *ser* → **era**, *ter* → **tinha**, *vir* → **vinha**, *pôr* → **punha**.
8. Future and progressive (units 11, 19)
9. Comparisons (unit 19)
10. Pronouns (units 1, 14)
Thirty verbs that cover most everyday conversation. The *eu* form and the past *eu* form are given because those two are the ones that most often break the pattern.

blocks.text: This course covers all of A1 Brazilian Portuguese grammar. What you have now is enough for everyday life: greeting people, ordering, asking the way, talking about yesterday and tomorrow, saying no politely, and complaining a little.
Three things this course deliberately **doesn't** touch, and which are your way into A2:

items: **Subjuntivo** — the form used for things that aren't certain: *espero que ele venha*, *se eu tivesse tempo*. It's the biggest grammar hurdle left, and it deserves its own time.
**Futuro do pretérito** — the "would" form: *eu iria*, *seria melhor*. You've already met one example, *deveria*, in unit 18.
**Two-verb combinations** — *pode ser que*, *acabei de chegar*, *estou para sair*. The combinations that make you sound grown-up.

blocks.text: But don't rush there. What matters most at this stage isn't the next grammar point but **flight hours**: listening and speaking until the forms you've learned come out without thinking.

blocks.title: How to keep going on your own
items: Listen for thirty minutes a day, even while doing something else. Brazilian podcasts for beginners, songs, telenovelas, YouTube channels. Your ears still need to get used to real speed.
Reread this course's dialogues out loud, one unit a day. You'll be surprised how much feels easy now compared with the first time.
Find one person to talk to regularly, even once a week. One hour of conversation beats ten hours of memorizing, and that's not a figure of speech.
Write five sentences a day about your own day, in the past tense. It's the cheapest exercise there is, and the one that pays off fastest.

blocks.text: *Errar faz parte.* Speak first, tidy up later. **Boa sorte, e até logo!**
